papers.notes: Paper IS SMOTE; there is no plain-SMOTE baseline. Proposed method as presented = SMOTE (k=5 nearest neighbours) combined with random majority under-sampling; ROC curves built by varying under-sampling at fixed SMOTE %. Comparisons: Under-C4.5 and Under-Ripper (plain under-sampling), Ripper Loss Ratio, Naive Bayes with varied priors (compared against SMOTE-C4.5), C4.5 decision thresholds (Phoneme), replication over-sampling (Mammography), SHRINK/one-sided selection (Oil, Tables 4-5, Acc+/Acc-). Only Table 3 gives per-dataset numbers (AUC, C4.5 only); Ripper and Naive Bayes results are ROC plots only (Figs 7-29) and AUCs for Ripper/Naive Bayes are explicitly not included. Table 5 (p.27, printed 347) gives Acc+/Acc- for 500% SMOTE + under-sampling 10%-800% on Oil vs Table 4 SHRINK 82.5%/60.9% and One-sided selection 76.0%/86.6%. Variants also introduced: SMOTE-NC (tested on Adult) and SMOTE-N (proposed, not tested). Paper notes exceptions: Pima (Naive Bayes dominates SMOTE-C4.5), Oil (Under-Ripper dominates SMOTE-Ripper), Can (overlap). A copy 'SMOTE (Original).pdf' exists in Binary folder; not read. papers.st: All seven main datasets (split into 48 two-class 'apportions') come from the UCR time series repository [17]. Seven further UCR datasets (CBF, Synthetic Control, OSU Leaf, Fish, Gun-Point, Trace, ECG) were used in an additional comparison whose results are only given online, not in the paper.
papers.cr: The datasets were chosen because they contain a large number of samples, to facilitate simulating scenarios of large class imbalance.
papers.pt: Started from seven 'balanced' UCR datasets. Multiclass sets (Adiac 37, FaceAll 14, 50words 50, SLeaf 15 classes) were made two-class by taking one class as positive and merging the rest as negative (one-vs-rest), giving several apportions per dataset (48 in total). The number of positive training samples was set to round numbers, no more than 50 percent of the available positives and no more than 50 per training set, to keep imbalance ratios high (7.6 to 60). Which classes were chosen as positive is not stated in the body text (Table 1 is an image).
papers.q: [p.2815] we constructed a total of 48 imbalanced two-class data apportions from seven balanced benchmark data sets in the UCR time series repository [17], as tabulated in Table 1.; [p.2815] seven balanced benchmark data sets in the UCR time series repository [17]; [p.2816] Out of the seven data sets, Adiac, FaceAll, 50words, and SLeaf originally contained 37, 14, 50, and 15 classes, respectively.

papers.st: KEEL dataset repository (24 multi-class sets, mostly UCI originals), with KEEL partitions.
papers.cr: A data set is considered imbalanced when one class has less than 40% of the majority class, that is IR > 1.5. The authors justify the selection because the base classifier and plain OVO/OVA get low performance on many of these sets, and note IR alone is not the only difficulty. The study covers many classes and a wide IR range, but IR is the global max/min ratio with no per-class minority definition.
papers.pt: Instances with missing values removed from autos, cleveland, dermatology and post-operative. 10-fold CV with KEEL partitions. Average accuracy as the measure.
papers.q: We have selected a wide benchmark of 24 multiple-class data-sets from the KEEL data-set repository. we consider a data-set to be imbalanced when one of its classes has a distribution of examples below 40% of the number of instances that belong to the majority class; that is, if the IR is higher than 1.5.

Metric: only average accuracy is reported per data-set in the paper; mean f-measure tables are said to be on the web page http://sci2s.ugr.es/multi-imbalanced/ (p.8), not fetched. No G-mean/AUC. Classifier C4.5 = first reported (abstract highlights none). SVM (Table 9, p.11) has no Base column; kNN in Table 11 p.12. OVA+SMT only aggregate (Table 4, p.8: C4.5 68.14). Table 8 p-values are for column method (OVO+preproc) vs row method; SMT vs Static-SMT C4.5 p=0.0357. Text layer verified with pdftotext -layout; tables were not images.

papers.st: 9 real-world datasets: 8 from the KEEL-dataset repository, plus acl, which the authors of ref. [45] (Slowinski et al.) supplied. 30 synthetic 2-D datasets (sub-cluster, clover, paw shapes; IR 5 or 7; 5 disturbance ratios) come from the family in ref. [40]/[46] and are on the paper's web page. 36 noisy versions were built by adding class or attribute noise (20%, 40%) to the 9 real-world datasets.
papers.cr: Real-world datasets: 'The choice of the real-world datasets was based on the work on imbalanced classification with noisy and borderline examples presented in [40]'; also 'As the number of noisy examples is quite high compared to the size of the minority class these data sets are chosen to study their impact.' Synthetic: 'This paper uses the family of synthetic datasets used in prior research on the role of borderline examples [40].'
papers.pt: Multi-class real-world datasets became binary by taking the union of one or more classes as positive and the rest as negative. Table 1 names each minority class (e.g. ecoli imU, newthyroid hyper, cleveland positive). Synthetic data were generated with 600 examples at IR=5 or 800 examples at IR=7, a minority class split into sub-regions (5 parts, or 3 for paw) inside a uniform majority, and borderline disturbance ratios DR = 0/30/50/60/70%. Noisy versions: class noise uses a pairwise scheme where a majority example is relabelled minority with probability x/100. Attribute noise: each attribute is corrupted separately in about x% of examples with a uniform random value (numeric) or a random domain value (nominal), x = 20% or 40%.
papers.q: [p.190 (printed)] This work focuses on binary classification problems (the minority versus the majority class) with examples randomly and uniformly distributed in the two-dimensional real-value space.; [p.191 (printed)] In such a way, 30 synthetic datasets with the above mentioned properties have been managed, all of which are available on the web-page associated with this paper.; [p.191 (printed)] In such a way, two different noise levels will be introduced into them: x = 20% and x = 40%. The introduction of noise consists of separately corrupting either the class labels or the attribute values

papers.q: 27 multiclass imbalanced data sets are used in our experiments. As there is no criterion to distinguish minority classes and majority classes in multiclass imbalance data, we simply classify the classes whose instances size greater (/smaller) than M/L as the majority (/minority) classes.

papers.st: 36 frequently used datasets in class-imbalance classification from the UCI and KEEL repositories.
papers.cr: The 36 datasets were chosen because they are frequently used in class-imbalance classification. They deliberately vary in size, imbalance ratio and number of features to test robustness under different situations. Many are nearly linearly separable and others heavily overlapped, which suits the overlap-based method.
papers.pt: 80:20 train/test split with 10-fold CV; Random Forest (500 trees) as classifier; binary datasets only.
papers.q: In all experiments, 36 frequently used datasets in class-imbalance classification were selected. These datasets are obtained from UCI and KEEL repositories, vary in terms of size (129 to 5472 instances), imbalance ratio (1.87 to 129.44), and number of features (3 to 19).

papers.st: MNIST (LeNet-5), CIFAR-10 (All-CNN), ILSVRC-2012 subset of ImageNet (ResNet-10, 1000 classes).
papers.cr: Three benchmarks of increasing complexity, all perfectly balanced in their original form, so imbalance can be induced in a fully controlled way and conclusions from a simple task can be checked on harder ones. Two imbalance profiles are defined: step imbalance (mu = fraction of minority classes, rho = majority/minority ratio) and linear imbalance. Minority classes are randomly chosen (MNIST, 50 repeats) or fixed as the lowest labels (CIFAR-10).
papers.pt: CIFAR-10: global contrast normalisation plus ZCA whitening, no augmentation. ImageNet: resize shorter side to 256, random 224x224 crop and mirroring, majority classes reduced from 1200 to 1000. All nets trained from scratch; multi-class ROC AUC.
papers.q: The first type is step imbalance. In step imbalance, the number of examples is equal within minority classes and equal within majority classes but differs between the majority and minority classes.
rows: other: MNIST benchmark (LeCun, Bottou, Bengio, & Haffner, 1998)

Each class uniformly at random subsampled to no more than 5000 training examples (balanced subset: 5000 train / 1000 test per class, Table 1; image 28x28x1), then artificially imbalanced (step and linear imbalance); minority classes randomized, 50 repetitions per setting; test set left balanced (Sec. 3.3.1, 3.4, p.4-5)
Original 5000 train / 1000 test per class (32x32x3); training set artificially imbalanced (step and linear); minority classes = lowest label values; test set left balanced (Sec. 3.3.2, p.4-5)

Majority classes reduced from 1200 to 1000 examples (1000 train / 50 test per class in balanced subset, Table 1; images rescaled, smaller side 256); classes with <1000 cases always chosen as minority; three step-imbalanced subsets, highest imbalance run 3 times with randomized minority classes (Sec. 3.3.3, p.5)

papers.irdef: ρ = max_i{|C_i|} / min_i{|C_i|} (ratio between number of examples in majority and minority classes, Eq. 2); step imbalance also uses µ = fraction of minority classes (Eq. 1); linear imbalance uses same ρ with linear interpolation of class sizes
papers.notes: Comparative study, not a new method: proposed = random minority oversampling ('Oversampling'). SMOTE not evaluated. All three datasets are 10- or 1000-class multiclass with artificially induced step/linear imbalance on the training set; test sets kept balanced. MNIST and CIFAR-10 results (Figs. 3-7) are plots only. Table 4 Undersampling values: 96.85, 94.98, 88.35, 84.08, 83.74. Supplementary Appendix A (CIFAR-10 reshuffled splits) contains plots only; Appendix B (convergence plots) and Appendix C (confusion matrices) not used for numeric comparison. Main comparator: Baseline (do-nothing).

papers.st: 12 UCI datasets; 19 KEEL imbalanced datasets; 10 simulated variations of MADELON generated with scikit-learn. Undersampled UCI variants add higher IR.
papers.cr: Not explicitly justified beyond using widely used public UCI and KEEL imbalanced benchmarks. Multiclass sets were binarised one-vs-rest (smallest class as minority) and undersampled to create higher-IR versions so the method is tested across a wide range of imbalance severity. Simulated MADELON data added as a difficult binary problem with high dimensionality and very low minority counts.
papers.pt: Multiclass binarised one-vs-rest; random undersampling of minority to raise IR; stratified 5-fold CV repeated 5 times; oversamplers balance to 1:1; grid search per metric.
papers.q: To evaluate k-means SMOTE, 12 imbalanced datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository are used. each of the aforementioned datasets was randomly undersampled to generate up to six additional datasets. Furthermore, 19 imbalanced datasets were selected from the KEEL repository.

papers.cr: Datasets chosen to expose the challenges of tabular generation: mixed discrete and continuous columns, multimodal continuous columns (57 of 123 continuous columns are multimodal) and highly imbalanced categorical columns (636 of 1048 categorical columns have a major category in over 90% of rows). Simulated data come from known oracles so likelihood fitness can be computed; real data have an ML task so ML efficacy is measured. Imbalance is natural, not induced.
papers.pt: Mode-specific normalisation of continuous columns with a variational Gaussian mixture; one-hot encoding of discrete columns; MNIST binarised; 300 epochs, batch 500.
papers.q: Our benchmark contains 7 simulated datasets and 8 real datasets.

papers.pt: 5-fold CV; training folds oversampled to perfect balance; undersampling of minority to create higher IR; LR, KNN, DT, GBC classifiers.
papers.q: UCI Machine Learning Repository, 13 datasets. KEEL repository, 13 datasets. Simulated data based on variations of the MADELON dataset, 2 datasets. Table 1 shows a summary of the final 69 data sets.

papers.st: MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR10, SVHN, CelebA (5 hair-colour classes, 64x64), LSUN (5 scene classes, 224x224 patch), SUN397 (50 random classes at 64x64).
papers.cr: Standard image benchmarks covering increasing difficulty and resolution. papers.q: All the chosen datasets except SUN397 are not significantly imbalanced in nature, therefore we have created their imbalanced variants by randomly selecting a disparate number of samples from the different classes.

papers.st: All from the KEEL imbalanced-data repository. Noise-corrupted versions are synthetic: label noise following Zhu et al. (majority-to-minority flips at 0 to 20%) and feature noise following Saez et al. (Gaussian noise per feature).
papers.cr: Datasets were chosen to vary in size, number of features and degree of imbalance, which the authors say ensures a reliable assessment. All are public KEEL sets, so they are reproducible. Noise levels were limited so the majority class never flips to minority, since oversampling to balance would otherwise be ill-defined.

papers.q: Overall, 34 two-class datasets with a varying level of imbalance were used throughout the experiments. Out of them, 10 were randomly chosen for the preliminary analysis, while the remaining 24 were used for the remainder of the experiments.

papers.q: The selection of the datasets was made based on the previous work by Saez et al., in which it was demonstrated that the chosen datasets possess various challenging characteristics, such as small disjuncts, frequent borderline and noisy instances, and class overlapping.

papers.st: Exp I: 66 simulated uniformly-distributed binary datasets (IR 1.5 to 120 x overlap 0 to 100% in steps of 10; negatives fixed at 6000, positives 50 to 4000). Exp II: 24 UCI/KEEL datasets. papers.cr: Simulated data were generated to control imbalance and overlap degree systematically, covering a wide range of scenarios including extreme imbalance and overlap. papers.q: In Experiment I, 66 uniformly-distributed binary-class datasets were simulated. In Experiment III, we used the breast cancer dataset from KDD Cup 2008 and the handwritten digits dataset from the MNIST database.

papers.st: 40 KEEL datasets; 10 large UCI datasets with over 4000 instances, two with over 160 features; 2 real datasets collected by the authors: Internet video traffic (Wireshark captures from 5 video sites, 256-dim BCD features) and esophageal cancer clinical text records (2861 records, 750-dim vectors after NLP).
papers.cr: KEEL datasets are a standard benchmark spanning low (IR<9, 12 sets) and high (IR>=9, 28 sets) imbalance. The UCI sets were chosen for being large (>4000 instances) and in two cases high-dimensional (>160 features) to test scalability and robustness beyond the small KEEL sets. The two real datasets show applicability to real imbalanced problems in network traffic and medical text.
papers.pt: 10-fold CV. Multi-class sets converted to binary with the smallest class as minority. Video-traffic features from BCD filtered with Weka CfsSubsetEval; esophageal text converted to 750-dim vectors by NLP.
papers.q: 40 public data sets from the KEEL data repository, and 10 large data sets from the UCI machine learning repository are used. Two real application data sets collected by ourselves are also used for the experiments.

papers.st: Own experiments: Yeast4, Yeast5, Yeast6 from UCI, each 10 attributes and about 1484 samples (51/44/35 minority).
papers.cr: The 3 datasets were chosen because they are routinely used by many oversampling methods, they are binary, and they stay imbalanced after some majority samples are hidden. The review's central argument is that oversampling is judged only by downstream classification metrics on a few benchmark datasets, with no check that synthesised samples are realistic.
papers.pt: Hide 10/25/50% of the majority class at random, oversample, then compare synthetic points to the hidden majority points with Hassanat distance; 5 repeats averaged.
papers.q: We employ three real-life datasets to put our validation system to the test, namely Yeast4, Yeast5, and Yeast6, which are routinely used by many oversampling methods.

papers.st: UCI and KEEL repositories. Balance, Breast-tissue, Cardiotocography, Cleveland, Dermatology, Glass, Hayesroth, Pageblock, UKM, Wine, Winequality-red/white, GesturePhase, Ecoli, Yeast, Segment, Texture and variants.
papers.cr: Standard UCI/KEEL multi-class benchmarks with 3 to 11 classes. Instances with missing values were removed, classes with fewer than 10 instances dropped, and class sizes adjusted in some datasets to obtain the required imbalance. Minority classes are not predefined: GLOS identifies them by comparing a class-level discreteness value with instance-level dispersion. The paper explicitly studies multi-minority, multi-majority and mixed cases by re-cutting Segment and Texture.
papers.pt: Removed missing-value instances; removed classes with fewer than 10 instances; adjusted class sizes in some datasets. C4.5 with OAA/OAO/OAHO/A&O decomposition. 5-fold CV x 10 runs.
papers.q: 21 multi-class data sets from the UCI repository and KEEL repository are selected. we removed the instances with missing values, removed the classes with less than 10 instances in each data set and adjusted the size of classes in some data sets.

papers.st: Widely used ordinal regression benchmark datasets plus UCI datasets. Examples: Toy, Stock10, Housing10, Abalone, LEV, SWD, Auto5, Voice3/6, Wisconsin5, Vertebral, Cleveland, Dermatology, Page-blocks, Yeast, Plates faults.
papers.cr: Real-world multiclass sets with 3 to 10 classes and varied class-size patterns. Several benchmarks are ordinal-regression sets that were discretised, which gives gradual class-size distributions. The class distribution of every dataset is listed with minority classes in bold. The rebalancing rule oversamples only classes whose imbalance degree exceeds 1.2.
papers.pt: Classes oversampled only if imbalance degree > 1.2, iteratively. Macro-F1, MG and MAUC with C4.5, NN and SVM.
papers.q: 21 multiclass real-world imbalanced datasets are selected for this experiment. They contain widely used ordinal regression benchmark datasets and UCI datasets.

papers.inh: SOUP paper and Lango & Stefanowski 2018
papers.st: Real data from UCI. Artificial datasets from the multi-imbalance Python toolbox (Grycza et al. 2020). The collection follows the SOUP paper and Lango & Stefanowski 2018.
papers.cr: Datasets were chosen to be diverse: multi-majority, multi-minority and gradual class-size configurations, different class overlap levels and different numbers of classes. The majority/minority labelling per class is taken from the SOUP paper, using two criteria: minority classes must be much smaller than majority ones, and the data-difficulty analysis of example safe levels must show that they are genuinely difficult.
papers.pt: Stratified 5-fold CV averaged over 10 runs. CART, NB, kNN, RF, GBT. Balanced accuracy, macro-F, G-mean, MCC, macro-AP.
papers.q: including problems with multi-majority, multi-minority, and gradual class size configurations; with different levels of class overlapping and with different numbers of classes, imbalance ratio from 2 to 164 and 27.6 on average.

papers.notes: Proposed method: GMMSampling (Naglik & Lango, Machine Learning 2024, 113:5183-5202). Ablation variants in Table 5 (p.17): without GMM, without undersampling, without Q_k, without P(x|k); Table 5 uses decision tree + G-mean (avg G-mean full method 0.6689). Per-dataset results for other classifiers and measures are in the online appendix at https://www.cs.put.poznan.pl/mlango/publications/GMMSampling.html (as printed, footnote 3, p.13) - not fetched. Table 3 (p.15) gives average ranks (DT, G-mean: Ours 2.33; S-SM 5.53; KM-SM 6.87). Implementation submitted to multi-imbalance library (https://github.com/damian-horna/multi-imbalance, as printed). Table 2 Average row printed: Ours 0.677; S-SM 0.646; KM-SM 0.632.

papers.inh: partial: synthetic generator from Vuttipittayamongkol et al. 2020
papers.st: UCI and KEEL repositories. Synthetic: 60 two-class sets with 1200 negatives, 6 to 400 positives, IR in {3,12,30,60,120,200} and overlap 0 to 90%, generated following Vuttipittayamongkol et al. (2020).
papers.cr: The paper targets class overlap, label noise and data scarcity. The 20 datasets span IR from 1.9 to 853 and 3 to 10 classes with multi-minority and multi-majority distributions. The synthetic sets give controlled IR x overlap grids, and the label-noise experiment randomly replaces labels at 5 to 30%. Minority/majority is determined per class from the class distribution rather than fixed.
papers.pt: 30 x 2-fold CV. RF main classifier (CART, MLP, KNN in the appendix). AvAcc, mean F-measure, CBA and CEN. Label noise added by random label replacement.
papers.q: Our experiment used 20 multi-class imbalanced datasets from UCI and KEEL repositories.

papers.st: UCI repository. Contraceptive Method Choice, User Knowledge Modeling, New-thyroid, Connect-4, Zoo, Cardiotocography, Ecoli, Glass Identification, Absenteeism at Work, Nursery, Letter Recognition, Car Evaluation, Wine Quality-White, Poker Hand, HCV, Yeast, Covertype, Chess (King-Rook vs King), Abalone, Bar Crawl, Avila.
papers.cr: Real, diverse UCI multi-class sets with varying imbalance. A class counts as a minority class if its IR_i = N_max/N_i exceeds 1.45, a threshold taken from a prior thesis to avoid over-oversampling mildly imbalanced classes. Multiple minority and multiple majority classes are handled simultaneously. Five-fold CV is used so every fold contains all classes, because some datasets are small.
papers.pt: 5-fold CV. CART and SVM in R with default parameters. MAUC and MG. dup_size=2, k=5.
papers.q: 21 multi-class imbalanced datasets from the UCI repository were utilized, IR_overall ranging from 1.65 to 391.52 and the IR values ranging from 1.89 to 87.47.

papers.notes: Proposed vs SMOTE only; other metric MAUC (Table 3, p.6) also per-dataset for CART and SVM, not extracted. SVM MG table is also in Table 4. Table 6 (p.8) k=3/5/7 sensitivity. Abstract says 'six imbalance problem handling methods and two classifiers' (baselines listed are 7 incl. ORI). Best_other excludes MKCS; includes ORI. Ties not specially handled (con: ORI/KSM tie 36.75 irrelevant). Avg row: ORI 43.62, MDO 64.40, KSM 42.58, RMS 68.89, FIY 76.83, MCC 66.90 (CART).

papers.st: Primary suite: 37 binary imbalanced KEEL datasets. Scale suite: 8 UCI datasets (Spambase, Waveform, Statlog Landsat, Musk v2, Page Blocks, Online Shoppers, HTRU2, Letter). Tuning suite: glass0, haberman, ecoli3, yeast3, abalone19.
papers.cr: Datasets, baselines, classifiers, metrics and tests were fixed in a preregistered protocol before running evaluation to avoid selective reporting. KEEL provides the standard imbalanced benchmark; 8 larger UCI datasets test generalisation beyond the KEEL regime and scalability. A disjoint tuning suite prevents leakage.
papers.pt: Per-fold standardisation fitted on the training fold; nominal attributes one-hot encoded; missing numeric values imputed with training-fold mean; multiclass binarised smallest-class-versus-rest; 4 classifiers; 11460 fold-level evaluations.
papers.q: The primary evaluation suite comprises 37 binary imbalanced datasets from the KEEL repository, with imbalance ratios from 1.8 to 41.4 and dimensions from 3 to 34. A scale suite of 8 larger datasets from the UCI repository, with sample sizes up to 20,000 and dimensions up to 166.

summary.tag_entries_note: an entry can carry several tags; these counts sum to more than the number of entries
summary.combinations_note: mutually exclusive; sums to the number of entries

interpretation: "Modified" is not one operation. Two operations account for almost all of it: redefining the task (class selection, mostly one-vs-rest) and deliberately raising the IR by removing minority examples. These change different things: the first changes what is being predicted, the second keeps the task but makes the minority scarcer.

The deliberate-IR group is concentrated in a few papers that generate several versions of each base set (factors x2..x20), so entry counts overstate how many distinct base data sets or papers are involved.

Most papers do not say why they modified data; when they do, the reasons are practical (the method is binary; test more extreme imbalance) rather than a claim that the modified version better represents an application.
Modification is not evidence of improper practice; the issue for interpretation is that a dataset name in a Modified entry does not identify the task or class distribution that was evaluated.
limits: Tags depend on the notes; where a note is silent about an operation the paper performed elsewhere, the tag is missing (the conditional field captures the known cases).
The purpose search is keyword-based (sentences containing a modification verb and a purpose phrase). A purpose expressed differently could be missed.

summary.t1_rule: T1 (Toon, 28 Oct 2026): names differing only by '-', '_', spaces or dots are one dataset; numbered or split versions belong to their main set's family; non-standard names are not merged (build/family_rule.py)

interpretation: **Concentrated?** Partly. Names are spread thin (half of all uses need 104 names; effective number about 264), so the literature is not dominated by a handful of names. At the level of base families the picture is more concentrated: 41 families carry half of all uses, and the 20 most used families carry 36%.

**Papers vs entries.** The distribution is almost the same in both units; the difference between "771 names" and "how much evidence" is mainly the long tail of single-paper names (546 names, one third of uses).

**Do the reused benchmarks cover different characteristics?** Within the reported values, the 30 most reused names are all small and low-dimensional: none has 10,000 or more instances or 100 or more features, while such data appear among the single-use and rarely used names. Larger and high-dimensional data in the corpus therefore come mainly from names few papers share.

**Underrepresented characteristics** that the data support: large (>= 10,000 instances) and high-dimensional (>= 100 features) data among the shared benchmarks. Domain or feature type cannot be assessed from this inventory (no field), so no claim is made about missing domains.
limits: 20% of entries lack instance counts and 24% lack feature counts; values are as printed and can differ across papers for the same name (see the size-variation finding: 78 of 198 names).
The family heuristic is coarse; it is used only to show the direction of the effect.
Reuse is not treated as a flaw: shared benchmarks make comparison across papers possible.

interpretation: The mix of data changes: early papers mostly modify UCI data themselves; from 2010 repository-defined (mainly KEEL) tasks appear and in 2020-2026 they are a third of entries, while modified entries fall to about a tenth. Part of what was "modification by the authors" earlier now arrives as a repository-defined task.
IR reporting becomes near universal (15% -> 92% of entries) and half of the later papers define their IR, while minority-class size is printed less often (45% -> 25%).
Entries whose origin cannot be told rise (5% -> 15%), and in 2020-2026 they supply 69 of 356 primary comparison rows.
All explicit import and identical-value baseline cases (B3, B4) are in 2020-2026; the B1 share is similar across periods (3/7, 10/21, 10/29).
Reliance on shared benchmarks is highest in 2020-2026 (48% of uses on names used by >= 5 papers).
The first period contributes only 3 papers with primary rows; comparisons of win shares across periods are not reported because the papers differ in metric, classifier and size.
limits: Period sizes differ (14 / 26 / 32 papers); entry-level shares are dominated by papers with many entries (e.g. k-means SMOTE, G-SMOTE).
The selection-rationale codes are ai_draft (not checked against the PDFs) and are shown only for orientation.
"Original" includes entries assigned by Toon's rules of 18 Oct (rule A and the multiclass common-name rule), which record reviewer judgement where the paper is silent.

crit.frequent: dataset papers >= 10 (datasets by rule T1-1: spellings that differ only by punctuation are one dataset; the 'datasets used by 10+ papers' set of Analysis C)
crit.diversity: dataset papers >= 3 and < 10, and every single-number value printed for it is >= 10,000 instances or every one is >= 100 features, printed in >= 2 papers; Analysis C found no entry of the 10+ set at or above these values
crit.verification: a listed candidate or pool name that meets neither rule, or whose printed values are too sparse or inconsistent to place it
crit.not_used: IR is not used to select candidates: definitions differ across papers (Analysis E); difficulty is not inferred from IR
crit.pool: the 11 names listed in the task + every name meeting the frequent or diversity rule

1. section นี้ต้องตอบอะไร

คำถามหลัก การที่วงการ SMOTE เลือกและจัดการข้อมูลแบบที่ทำกันอยู่ ส่งผลต่อความน่าเชื่อถือของผลลัพธ์ที่รายงานอย่างไร
และควรปรับการประเมินผลอย่างไรในงานถัดไป

ไม่ใช่ การสรุปว่า paper ไหนใช้ dataset กี่ชุด ตัวเลขนั้นอย่างเดียวไม่มีประโยชน์

แกนการนำเสนอที่อาจารย์กำหนด แบ่งตาม paper ก่อน แล้วจำแนกข้อมูลที่แต่ละ paper ใช้เป็น 3 แบบ

แบบความหมาย
Originalbenchmark มาตรฐาน (UCI / KEEL) ใช้ตามที่แจกมา ไม่ดัดแปลง
Modifiedดัดแปลงเอง เช่น binarize จาก multiclass, รวมคลาส, สุ่มตัด minority เพื่อดัน IR, ใส่ noise
Syntheticผู้เขียนสร้างขึ้นเอง

ป้ายที่ใช้จริงตอนนี้ (18 ต.ค.) 4 แบบ + not stated: original, repository-defined (KEEL หรือ imbalanced-learn เป็นผู้แบ่งคลาส), modified, synthetic
repository-defined คือทางเลือกที่ 3 ของ decisions-pending เรื่องที่ 2 ใช้ระหว่างรออาจารย์ ยุบกลับเป็น 3 แบบได้ที่ keel_rule()

แล้วดูว่าแต่ละ paper "ชนะ" บนข้อมูลแบบไหน

สมมติฐาน

  • H1 อัตราการชนะบนข้อมูล Modified และ Synthetic สูงกว่าบนข้อมูล Original (ข้อสังเกตของ Toon อาจารย์รับแล้ว)
  • H2 paper ที่ใส่ชุดมาตรฐานมาแค่ชุดเดียวเพื่อความน่าเชื่อถือ มักรายงานผลที่อยากได้จากข้อมูลอีกแบบ (ข้อสังเกตของอาจารย์)
  • H3 dataset ที่ปรากฏในตารางคุณลักษณะ แต่ไม่ปรากฏในตารางผล (ข้อสังเกตของ Toon ตั้งเป็นสมมติฐานเพิ่ม)

การทดสอบใช้ mixed-effects logistic regression ให้ paper เป็น random effect เพราะ dataset ภายใน paper เดียวกันไม่เป็นอิสระต่อกัน
Fisher exact ใช้เป็นตัวอ้างอิงหยาบเท่านั้น

2. เหตุผลที่ร่างแรกไม่ผ่าน และข้อกำหนดที่ตามมา

อาจารย์ไม่ผ่านร่างแรกเพราะอ่านแล้วเหมือน AI เขียน คำพูดคือ "เอา 80 paper โยนให้ AI เขียน ใครก็ทำได้"

ข้อกำหนดที่ตามมา ทั้งหมดนี้บังคับ

  1. ต้องมี insight ของ Toon เอง ไม่ใช่บทสรุปที่เครื่องสร้าง
  2. ทุกค่าที่มาจาก AI ต้องเปิด paper ต้นฉบับตรวจเอง
  3. ต้องเริ่มจาก "สิ่งที่เราสงสัย" แล้วหาหลักฐานมาตอบ ไม่ใช่เริ่มจากตารางสรุป

ผลต่อวิธีทำงานในโฟลเดอร์นี้ ทุกแถวในฐานข้อมูลที่ AI เติมให้จะถูกตั้งสถานะ ai_draft (unverified) และ ไม่มี page_ref
สคริปต์วิเคราะห์จะข้ามแถวเหล่านี้ทิ้งโดยอัตโนมัติ แถวจะนับก็ต่อเมื่อ Toon เปิด paper ตรวจแล้วเปลี่ยนสถานะเป็น
verified against paper หรือ corrected พร้อมใส่เลขหน้าและตาราง

ข้อสรุปทั้งหมดของ Data section (SMOTE25)

ฉบับ 29 ต.ค. 2026 · Claude เขียนตามที่ Toon มอบหมาย ("อะไรที่ต้องตัดสินใจ ตัดสินใจเลย") · ตัวเลขทุกตัวในไฟล์นี้มาจากไฟล์ใน out/ และ difficulty/ ที่ระบุไว้ท้ายแต่ละหัวข้อ และตรงกับ manuscript/data-section-draft.tex (ตรวจด้วย build/consistency_check.py)

0. สิ่งที่ Claude ตัดสินแทนคืนนี้ (Toon ควรอ่านส่วนนี้ก่อน)

เรื่องตัดสินว่าถ้าไม่เห็นด้วย แก้ที่
นิยาม win/lossใช้นิยามที่ Toon ตัดสิน 28 ต.ค.: ทุก metric ที่ paper รายงานคู่กับ SMOTE, classifier/เงื่อนไขตามกติกา A, เทียบค่าที่พิมพ์, เท่ากัน = เสมอ · กติกา A (metric เดียว) เหลือเป็นการตรวจความทนทานbuild/winloss_allmetric.py
ป้ายตัวเทียบใน all-metricแก้ความไม่สอดคล้อง: เมื่อวาน all-metric ติดป้าย GAMO, MC-CCR, MC-RBO, NROMM, RBBoost, KNNOR เป็น plain SMOTE แต่ชุดกติกา A (ตรวจ 18–19 ต.ค.) จัดเป็น SMOTE แบบห่อ / ค่าเฉลี่ย / ข้ามตาราง · ใช้การจัดของกติกา A ทั้งสองชุด → plain 29 paper (เดิม 35)COMPARATOR_GROUP, EXCLUDED ใน build/winloss_allmetric.py
ป้าย KEEL 2 คลาส (decisions-pending 2)คง repository-defined แยก (ทางเลือก 3 ที่ Toon ใช้อยู่)keel_rule() ใน build/full_extraction.py
H3 / granularity (decisions-pending 3)ใช้ 6 ระดับ และวัด H3 เป็นสัดส่วน entry ที่ลิสต์แต่ไม่มีคู่ค่ากับ SMOTEbuild/hypotheses.py
วิธีทดสอบ H1ตาม handoff: paper เป็น cluster · GEE (หลัก), conditional logit ภายใน paper, Bayesian mixed model (paper + dataset), Fisher เป็นค่าอ้างอิงหยาบ · α = 0.05 สองทาง (มาตรฐาน)build/hypotheses.py
H2นิยาม: paper ที่มีชุดมาตรฐาน 1 ชุดพอดี + ชุดอื่น ≥ 1 · เข้าเกณฑ์ 2 paper จึงรายงานราย paper ไม่ทดสอบbuild/hypotheses.py
ประโยคสีน้ำเงิน 9 จุด + ช่อง [Toon] 4 ช่องเขียนเป็นข้อความฉบับสุดท้ายทั้งหมด ทุกจุดมีคอมเมนต์ % Claude 29 Oct 2026 (Toon delegated all open decisions) ให้ค้นได้manuscript/data-section-draft.tex
ชุด dataset อ้างอิง (ข้อ 15)ใส่ใน manuscript (ตาราง tab:data-reference) คง 27 task ไม่ตัดตระกูลซ้ำ แต่เขียนเตือนให้รวมตามแหล่งเวลาทดสอบdifficulty/reference_collection.py
สิ่งที่ไม่ได้ทำไม่ merge เข้า main.tex / sections / references.bib (กติกา: แก้เฉพาะ Data section) แต่ทำฉบับพร้อม merge และคอมไพล์กับ template จริงผ่านแล้ว · ไม่ pushดูหัวข้อ 11

  • อ่านว่า: ผลชนะ SMOTE ที่รายงานไว้มีแนวโน้มอยู่บนข้อมูลที่ minority เป็น borderline/outlier มาก ไม่ใช่บนข้อมูลที่ IR สูง

8. ข้อแนะนำ 8 ข้อ (ใน manuscript ทุกข้อชี้กลับไปที่หัวข้อ)

  1. บอก repository, version, ทั้งชุดหรือไฟล์ train
  2. บอกคลาส minority และเหตุผลในเนื้อความ
  3. ประกาศการดัดแปลงทุกแบบ และพิมพ์ขนาด/จำนวนคลาสของชุดที่ใช้จริง
  4. บอกสูตร IR
  5. รายงานจำนวน source family คู่กับจำนวน dataset และรวม split ของแหล่งเดียวกันเวลาทดสอบนัยสำคัญ
  6. รายงานผลรายชุดเทียบ plain SMOTE ทุก metric แยกชุดมาตรฐานกับชุดดัดแปลง
  7. แยกชุดจูนกับชุดวัดผล และรัน baseline เอง
  8. รายงานตัววัดว่า minority อยู่ตรงไหน (safe/borderline/rare/outlier) คู่กับ IR

9. ข้อจำกัดที่ต้องเขียนไว้

  • ผลชนะเป็นการเทียบค่าที่ paper พิมพ์ ไม่ใช่การทดลองซ้ำ และสเกลเทียบข้าม paper ไม่ได้ (ใช้ paper เป็น cluster ทุกโมเดล)
  • หน่วย dataset × metric ให้น้ำหนัก paper ที่รายงานหลาย metric มากกว่า จึงรายงานหนึ่งผลต่อ dataset และกติกา A คู่กันเสมอ
  • metric อื่นนอกจาก metric ของกติกา A อ่านจาก PDF ครั้งเดียว (ไม่มีการลอกซ้ำอิสระ)
  • ความยากวัดจากไฟล์ mirror (keel-ds, imbalanced-databases, PMLB + 8 พ.ย.: KEEL standard 2 ชุด, UCI++, Weka-UCI, PROMISE, jbrownlee); 72 ไฟล์ KEEL ตรงกับตารางทางการ, KEEL standard สองชุดตรงกัน 67/67 ไฟล์ ที่เหลือยังไม่ได้เทียบเพราะเข้าเว็บ KEEL/UCI ไม่ได้
  • การเชื่อมความยากกับผลชนะเป็น exploratory (89 ไฟล์ 22 paper ไฟล์เล็ก มิติต่ำ)
  • H2 มีแค่ 2 paper

wl_all.rule:
(no threshold): compare the printed numbers. win = proposed better in the
metric's direction, loss = worse, tie = printed values equal. Rows with a non-numeric value

sections.reader: เห็นผลชนะแยกตามชนิดข้อมูล และรู้ว่า paper ไหนพิสูจน์บนข้อมูลมาตรฐาน
found: ระดับ paper: 44 paper ใช้ plain SMOTE เป็น baseline, 13 ใช้ SMOTE แบบอื่น, 16 ไม่เทียบ

นิยาม win/loss ของ Toon (28 ต.ค.): ทุก metric, เทียบค่าที่พิมพ์, เท่ากัน = เสมอ · 29 paper 524 dataset 1,511 แถว (ตัดสินได้ 1,495 แถว 520 dataset): วิธีที่เสนอชนะ 1,107 เสมอ 102 แพ้ 286 (เทียบไม่ได้ 16) = ชนะ 79.5% ของที่ตัดสินได้; 23/29 paper มีแถวที่ SMOTE ชนะ
แยก metric (ชนะ/ตัดสินได้): AUC/G-mean/F/recall 76–83%, accuracy 91%, MCC 83% แต่ precision 62:46 และ specificity SMOTE ชนะ 6/7
ความทนทาน: หนึ่งผลต่อ dataset 409/35/76; กติกา A (metric เดียว) 521 แถว: วิธีที่เสนอชนะ 402 เสมอ 39 แพ้ 80

H1 ไม่ได้รับการสนับสนุน: modified+synthetic ชนะ 75.7% vs original 79.4%; GEE OR 0.69 (p 0.10), ภายใน paper OR 0.62 (p 0.04), mixed 0.75; ไม่ทนเมื่อใช้หนึ่งผลต่อ dataset หรือกติกา A; ราย paper 4 vs 7 (sign p 0.55)
H2: เข้าเงื่อนไขแค่ 2 paper (MWMOTE, RUSBoost) ชนะบนข้อมูลอื่น 80.0% เท่ากับ paper อื่น 80.3% ทดสอบไม่ได้

SMOTE แบบอื่น 12 paper 558 แถวรายงานแยก (Static-SMOTE 79, OVO 148, SMOTE-all 239, ห่อกับ learner อื่น 92) · ตัดออก KNNOR (ค่าเฉลี่ย), RBBoost (ข้ามตาราง), MC-MBRC (หัวคอลัมน์ไม่ระบุ SMOTE)

sections.reader: รู้ว่า paper ไหนพิสูจน์ผิดไม่ได้จากสิ่งที่ตีพิมพ์ และ baseline ไหนถูกยกมาแทนการรันใหม่

manuscript.html:
How the SMOTE Literature Uses Data

A reader who wants to compare two SMOTE variants, or to choose a benchmark for a new one, needs answers to questions that the papers rarely answer together. Can the numbers that two papers report on a dataset of the same name be compared? How broad is the evidence behind the benchmarks the field relies on? How difficult, beyond the imbalance ratio, are the datasets that can be checked? When a paper reports that its method beats SMOTE, on what kind of data does that happen, and can a reader check it? This section answers these questions from the 1,747 dataset entries and the comparisons with SMOTE that we extracted from the 76 papers of our corpus: 835 under one fixed metric per paper (834 per dataset and one average over datasets) and 2,497 over every metric the papers report. Three of them (ENN, AdaBoost and one review) contain no evaluation on data, so counts below use the 73 papers with an evaluation on data; Tomek links is kept because it illustrates its method on one synthetic two-class set.

The central observation is that the evidence for a new oversampler is only as interpretable as the description of its data, and in this literature that description is often incomplete: the same name can denote different tasks, many modifications are not described well enough to be repeated, and 14 of the 57 papers that use SMOTE as a baseline give no per-dataset pair of scores against it. Where per-dataset results exist, the proposed method beats plain SMOTE in about four of five decided comparisons. These wins are not more frequent on data the authors modified, but they are more frequent on data whose minority examples are borderline or isolated, and they are much less consistent on precision and specificity than on the other metrics.

Extraction Procedure

For every paper we read the full text and any supplementary file in our collection, and recorded each dataset as printed, including spelling, with its group in the paper, source repository, size, number of features and classes, minority and majority counts, and the imbalance ratio where the paper prints them, together with the table and page they come from. For each dataset we also recorded how it reached the experiment: original (used as distributed, with its native classes), repository-defined (a two-class split published by a repository such as KEEL or imbalanced-learn, used as is), modified (the authors chose the minority classes, merged or dropped classes, set a threshold, undersampled or injected noise), or synthetic (generated by the authors). Where a paper did not state its source, two fixed rules were applied and flagged: names that follow the KEEL file convention (for example ecoli-0-1_vs_5, yeast4) were labelled repository-defined, and common names in multiclass papers with no stated change were labelled original. Two further rules were fixed before counting: a set that is two-class in its source and is used without comment was labelled original, and a set from which the authors removed rows (for example, records with missing values) or attributes was labelled modified. A set whose source the paper does not state, for which it prints no size, and whose name identifies a public unmodified file was labelled original (four entries). One label rests on evidence outside the paper: the toy set of OREM-M, listed without a source, is the synthetic set of the ordinal-regression benchmark [gutierrez2016ordinal] and is labelled synthetic.

For the results we copied, per dataset, the printed score of the proposed method and of SMOTE from one results table selected by a fixed rule: G-mean, else AUC, else F-measure, else accuracy; the classifier highlighted in the abstract, else the first reported; the unperturbed condition. We recorded values rather than wins so that any definition of a win can be applied later. From the same table setting we then copied every other metric that the paper reports for both methods (2,497 dataset-by-metric values in 44 papers); the fixed-metric values were copied a second time in this pass, independently, and agree on all 839 rows that both copies contain. Plain SMOTE was distinguished from SMOTE embedded in a multiclass or ensemble wrapper (Static-SMOTE, OVO-SMOTE [fernandez2013analysing], SMOTE-all, SMOTE+AdaBoost). Values printed in a paper are never overwritten; corrections against the source repository are stored beside them with their justification. Every extracted value was then checked against the PDF a second time: a value was accepted when the dataset name and its numbers appear on the same line of the cited page, and every table that is printed as an image or whose text layer is garbled was read from the rendered page instead. All 1,654 dataset entries of the first extraction and 835 fixed-metric comparisons passed this check (the 93 sets added on 8 November were checked the same way, with a quoted sentence on the cited page); the values of the other metrics were read once, from the text layer or the rendered page.

Evidence: ai-draft/full/SCHEMA.md; build/full_extraction.py; KEEL and multiclass rules approved by Toon 18 Oct, rules A and B 18 Oct; 454 extraction notes in out/full_uncertain.csv, each resolved in out/uncertain_resolution.csv; second check: build/verify_pdf.py, out/visual_checks.json, out/verified_*.csv; values also checked by Toon against the PDFs (28 Oct 2026).

The Benchmark Landscape

The 73 papers with an evaluation on data list 1,747 dataset entries, counting the 93 sets that ten papers generate only for an illustration or a side experiment (Section 1.7). One of them, the single toy example in Tomek links, is a description rather than a name and is set aside here, leaving 1,746 named entries. These reduce to 857 distinct names once names are lower-cased, text in parentheses is dropped, and underscores and spaces are treated alike. Treating spellings that differ only in punctuation as one dataset (page-blocks, pageblocks and the singular page-block) leaves 766 datasets, and grouping each numbered or split version with its main set (for example yeast4 or glass-0-1-6_vs_2 with yeast and glass), while keeping non-standard names such as glass identification apart, leaves 482 source families. Most datasets appear once: 543 of the 766 occur in a single paper (60 of them are the generated sets of a single experiment in MC-MBRC [ma2024mcmbrc], which form one family). Counted as datasets, ecoli appears in 29 papers, yeast in 22 and glass in 19; counted with their splits, the ecoli family appears in 42 papers, the yeast family in 39 and the glass family in 35, about half of the 73. Half of all uses of a family fall on 40 of the 482 families. Names whose printed number of features contradicts their main set are kept in its family when they are the same source with a different composition (for example abalone8, oil1) and kept apart when they are a different data set that shares the prefix (for example car1, a microarray set with 9,182 features).

Splits cut from one source are not copies of each other. Among the verifiable two-class KEEL files (Section 1.5), the 14 yeast splits range in imbalance ratio from 2.5 to 41.4 and in noise index from 0.29 to 0.86, and the 19 ecoli and 13 glass splits from 0.12 to 0.69 and from 0.24 to 0.77. They do share the source’s attributes (7 or 8 for yeast, 6 or 7 for ecoli, 9 for glass), its domain and often its examples: yeast4 and yeast-0-5-6-7-9_vs_4 use the same 51 minority examples and differ only in which classes form the majority.

Outcomes on splits of one source are also related. In the eleven papers that compare with plain SMOTE on several splits of the same source (282 per-dataset comparisons, 262 same-family pairs; families by the rule in the evidence note), whether the proposed method wins does not cluster by family (pairs agree on win, tie or loss in 0.60 of cases, as under random relabelling), but the size of its margin does: the within-paper ranks of the margin differ by 0.29 on average for two splits of one source against 0.34 when family labels are permuted within each paper (\(p = 0.005\), 10,000 permutations; leaving out one paper at a time gives \(p\) between 0.002 and 0.048).

Splits cut from one source vary the task (its imbalance ratio and where the minority examples lie) but not the source (its domain, attributes and dimensionality), and within the papers that evaluate several splits of one source, the margin over SMOTE tends to be slightly more alike within a family than between families. Papers should therefore report the number of source families alongside the number of datasets, and should not treat each split as independent evidence.

What the reader should do.

Report the source family of each dataset alongside the count, so that readers can see how many independent sources stand behind a claim, and keep splits of one source together when testing for significance.

Evidence: out/verified_datasets.csv; counts reproduced by build/reconcile_counts.py (out/reconcile_counts.json): rule R1 sets aside the Tomek links placeholder (row 1558, kept in the file), R2 normalises with build/analyse_dataset_usage.py norm(), R3 gives exact-name, dataset and family counts under rule T1 (build/family_rule.py, out/dataset_families.csv; the earlier prefix count gave 39/39/36 and is superseded); datasets and families per name: out/landscape_families.csv; concentration by dataset and family: out/benchmark_concentration.json. With the placeholder the counts are 858 and 627; removing all punctuation would leave 678 names. The 605 names of the 6 Oct list are superseded by the 771 of the full re-read (857 after the 93 generated sets of build/add_synthetic_entries.py, 8 Nov 2026). Spread within the yeast, ecoli and glass families: difficulty/family_spread.py \(\rightarrow\) family_spread.json. Datasets and families everywhere in this subsection: rule T1 (Toon, 28 Oct 2026; names differing only by punctuation are one dataset, numbered or split versions belong to their main set, non-standard names are not merged), build/family_rule.py \(\rightarrow\) out/dataset_families.csv; outcomes linked to records through out/outcome_dataset_links.csv; build/family_dependence.py \(\rightarrow\) out/family_dependence.json (key t1).

Candidate benchmarks for a cross-family comparison.

Table 1 lists 18 datasets considered as benchmarks for comparing method families: the 11 datasets we set out to examine and the datasets that meet one of two written rules. The first rule takes every dataset used by at least ten papers (33 datasets). The second takes datasets used by three to nine papers whose every printed size is at least 10,000 instances, a size that no entry of the first group reaches (7 datasets). The groups follow from these two rules on use and printed size only and say nothing about overlap, noise, sparsity, feature type or any other property. IR is not used, because its definition differs between papers. No dataset used by three or more papers is printed with 100 or more features every time it is reported; this is a property of the rule, not evidence that the corpus contains no high-dimensional data sets.

Family counts follow the same rule for every dataset. The dataset shuttle is printed with four different sizes (2,175, 14,500, 43,500 and 57,999 instances) and once without a size. Two pairs of papers print matching sizes and class counts; the other versions are single reports, and OVO-SMOTE prints five classes in one table and seven class counts in another. The versions are therefore kept apart and not pooled.

The frequently used benchmarks are small: among the entries that print a size, half have 800 or fewer instances and half have nine or fewer features. Names printed with 10,000 or more instances in every paper are used by three to nine papers each, so a comparison across method families that wants to cover data size has to look beyond the frequent set.

Limits of the evidence.

Size, dimensionality and the number of classes are printed for 75.9%, 72.7% and 78.4% of the 1,746 named entries, and class proportions in some form for 54.8%. A measured class overlap exists for 36 entries in two papers, on two incompatible scales, and the curated evidence contains no statement about sparsity. What the papers print therefore cannot show which ranges of overlap, noise or sparsity the benchmarks cover; the candidates in Table 1 are chosen on use and size only. Section 1.5 measures these properties directly for the entries whose files can be identified.

Evidence: out/benchmark_candidates.csv and .json (build/landscape_candidates.py; rules and approval status in criteria); table rows written by build/landscape_manuscript.py; out/landscape_families.csv (446 groups, 82 flagged and left unmerged); out/shuttle_versions.csv (build/shuttle_versions.py; OVO-SMOTE Table 2 and Table 3, p.6, checked 19 Oct); out/characteristics_coverage.json; out/benchmark_concentration.json. All records are browsable in the Atlas (manuscript tab and Landscape tab).

How Datasets Are Chosen and Modified

Table 2 shows that modification by the authors is common: 332 of 1,747 dataset entries were changed by the authors themselves, and for 195 the paper does not let a reader tell how the data were obtained. Eleven papers give no reason for their choice of datasets or only call them widely used.

Modification is not a fault in itself: binarising a multiclass set or raising the imbalance ratio are legitimate ways to probe a method. What matters for the reader is whether the modification is declared where a reader looks for it. A KEEL file name such as yeast-0-5-6-7-9_vs_4 declares its split; a paper that prints only “Yeast” after choosing its own minority classes does not.

Modifications differ in how completely they are described. Of the 332 modified entries (39 papers), 177 in 30 papers change the class structure, most often by keeping one class against the rest (84 entries), and 147 in 9 papers raise the imbalance ratio on purpose, almost always by removing minority examples at random (131 entries). A purpose for the change is stated in 15 of the 39 papers. For 94 of the 332 entries, information needed to repeat the change is missing: the characteristics of the modified set are not printed for 56, the target imbalance ratio for 18 and the minority class for 15. At the paper level, 8 of the 37 papers that binarise data do not state which class becomes the minority. Entries modified without printed characteristics cannot be matched to any public file unless the authors publish the modified data themselves, as k-means SMOTE does; 48 such entries are therefore left out of the difficulty measurement (Section 1.5).

Evidence: out/data_handling_summary.json (paper-level codes; binarised_without_stated_rule, minority_rule_among_binarised); out/full_summary.json how_obtained_all (entry level, with rules); operations, purposes and missing information: build/modified_operations.py \(\rightarrow\) out/modified_operations_audit.csv and out/modified_operations_summary.json (Analysis A).

The Same Name Is Not the Same Data

Of the 192 datasets that at least two papers print with a size (spellings that differ only in punctuation counted as one dataset), 90 appear with more than one size: thyroid with 7,200 instances in five papers and 720 in four, dermatology with 358 (the KEEL version) in eight and 366 (UCI) in two, ecoli with 336, 327, 310 and 301, and pima with 768, 769, 635 and 590. Some of these differences are declared subsamples; the name alone does not tell which. MWMOTE [barua2014mwmote] illustrates the problem inside a single paper: its Satimage (6,435 instances) and Statlandsat (4,435) are the full Statlog Landsat set and its training file, counted as two of its twenty datasets, and its common names are ambiguous in both directions (its Ecoli matches the KEEL file ecoli1 exactly, while its Yeast matches no published split).

Imbalance ratios add a second layer. Table 3 lists the definitions found in the corpus; some are not convertible into one another, and some papers print IR without a formula.

What the reader should do.

Compare results across papers only after mapping each name to its exact file and class split, and report the IR formula together with its values.

Evidence: out/verified_datasets.csv: names normalised, printed n_instances compared across papers (192 datasets, rule T1, with a printed size in two or more papers; 198 if spellings are kept apart; out/reconcile_counts.json size_variation); the earlier 20 of 75 from ai-draft/dataset_variants.json covered 8 papers only and is superseded; mwmote-table5-audit.md; extraction-notes.md; full re-read ir_definition per paper in out/full_summary.json.

How Difficult Are the Datasets That Can Be Checked?

The papers rarely describe how hard their data are beyond the imbalance ratio. A numerical overlap measure is printed for 36 of the 1,746 named entries, all in two papers, and noise or borderline examples are described for 5; three of 72 papers report such a property of their original data (Section 1.2). The literature on imbalanced learning, however, attributes much of the difficulty of these problems to characteristics of the data other than the imbalance ratio: overlap between the classes, noisy and borderline examples, small disjuncts and a shortage of minority examples [jo2004smalldisjunctslopez2013insightnapierala2016types]. We therefore measured these characteristics ourselves on the entries whose data can be identified. An entry counts as verifiable when its name matches a public file and the printed number of instances (and of minority examples, when printed) equals that file’s, or when the paper prints no size, the name matches a public file and the authors did not modify the data, or when the authors publish the modified file themselves under the entry’s name (k-means SMOTE [douzas2018kmeans]). One paper (Loyalty-SMOTE) prints, for eight entries, a size exactly one larger than the public file, apparently counting the header line; for this paper a printed size of the file’s size plus one is accepted. A two-class file is not accepted for an entry whose paper prints more than two classes. The files come from KEEL [alcalafdez2011keel], the UCI repository [kellyucirepository] (downloaded from the repository, and through the UCI++ collection [garciaucipp], the UCI files distributed with Weka and single-file copies), LIBSVM [chang2011libsvm], PMLB [romano2022pmlb], imbalanced-learn [lemaitre2017imbalanced], the PROMISE defect data [jureczko2010towards] and the repositories in which five papers publish their own processed data, and Kaggle for the sets that papers take from it. A name is looked up under the other published names of the same data set (liver disorders is bupa, contraceptive method choice is cmc), but only the printed size decides whether a file is accepted. This holds for 986 entries from 65 papers, which use 256 files. Entries modified by their authors without printed characteristics and without a published file (48) are left out, because the data actually used cannot be reconstructed.

Each two-class file, each binarisation that a paper describes precisely enough to reproduce, and each imbalanced-learn task defines one task: 236 tasks, used by 701 entries in 46 papers. One-vs-rest tasks that we built from multiclass files (339) are not tasks any paper evaluated and are reported apart. Every minority example is labelled safe, borderline, rare or outlier from the classes of its five nearest neighbours [napierala2016types], with distances measured by HVDM [wilson1997improved]. The noise index of a task is the share of minority examples that are borderline or outliers; we report it as a continuous value because we found no published threshold for it. Three flags use published thresholds: small disjuncts when at least 20% of minority examples are rare and outliers when more than 20% are outliers [napierala2016types], and small sample when there are fewer than ten minority examples per feature [jain2000statistical]. The imbalance ratio \(N_{\mathrm{maj}}/N_{\mathrm{min}}\), computed from the files, is grouped into the bands 1.5 to 3, 3 to 9 and above 9 [fernandez2008study] and is not used as a difficulty flag.

Table 4 shows that the most common property of the binary tasks is a small sample: 160 of 236 have fewer than ten minority examples per feature. The flags combine in seven profiles: small sample alone (87 tasks), small sample with outliers (42), all three flags (28), outliers alone (11), small disjuncts with a small sample (3), small disjuncts with outliers (2) and none (63). The noise index separates tasks that the flags do not (Figure 1a): among the 63 tasks without a flag it ranges from 0 to 0.84, with 20 tasks at 0.5 or above (haberman 0.84, the numeric German credit data 0.81, contraceptive 0.79 and bupa 0.79 among them) and 16 below 0.1. Its median is 0.31, 0.44, 0.48 and 0.66 in the imbalance-ratio bands up to 1.5 (6 tasks), 1.5 to 3 (40), 3 to 9 (51) and above 9 (139), and its rank correlation with the imbalance ratio is 0.26.

The measurable part of the corpus is also low-dimensional (Figure 1b). The printed number of features has a median of 9 and half of the entries lie between 4 and 10 features. The 59 entries with more than 100 features come from 54 names in 18 papers, no name is used by more than two papers, and only six of them could be verified (musk twice, isolet, and madelon, a1a and mushrooms in the files that HDE publishes); the verified tasks have at most 617 features (median 9).

The imbalance ratio, the one difficulty-related number most papers print, says little about where the minority examples lie: tasks with a low ratio can be as mixed as tasks with a high one, and a task without any flag is not necessarily easy. Conclusions drawn from the common benchmarks speak mainly for small, low-dimensional tables with few minority examples per feature.

Most papers mix these profiles. Of the 39 papers with at least three verifiable tasks, 36 include both flagged and flag-free tasks, two (COG-OS [wu2007cogos] and SMOTE-ENN) use only flag-free tasks and one (GOIO) only flagged ones. Section 1.6 relates the measured profiles to the reported wins.

A reference collection.

For readers who need a small benchmark that covers the measured range, Table 5 selects 42 of the 236 tasks by a fixed rule with no threshold of our own. Each combination of flag profile and imbalance-ratio band that occurs (19 combinations) contributes the task that the corpus uses most, for comparability with earlier results, and the tasks with the lowest and the highest noise index, for spread. The collection spans noise indices from 0 to 1, imbalance ratios from 1.1 to 970.6 and sizes from 79 to 62,630 instances, and 13 of its files match the official KEEL table. Its tasks are not independent of one another: it holds four yeast splits, three pima versions and two each of ecoli, glass, haberman, cleveland, heart and iris, which should be grouped by source when results are tested.

Limits of the measurement.

Part of the files are copies of the repositories rather than downloads from the repositories themselves: the keel-ds and imbalanced-databases packages, two independent GitHub copies of the KEEL standard collection, PMLB, UCI++, the UCI files distributed with Weka, a copy of the tera-PROMISE defect data and single UCI files from a public data-set mirror. The UCI and LIBSVM files added in the second pass were downloaded from the repositories, and five papers’ own files from the repositories their authors name (HDE, DGOT, SOS, MBS and the k-means SMOTE release). Nine Kaggle data sets that papers name were downloaded from their Kaggle pages; Kaggle files are uploaded by users, and a file may differ from the one a paper used. For the 72 KEEL files in the official KEEL table, instance and feature counts match in every case, and the two copies of the KEEL standard collection agree in instances and features on all 67 files they share; the other files have not been compared with the repositories. When several copies hold the same data set, each entry added in the second pass is mapped to one copy, the authors’ own files and KEEL first and PMLB last, because PMLB stores nominal attributes as integer codes, which then enter HVDM as numeric attributes. Rows with missing values are dropped before the neighbours are found; the largest losses are 1,129 of the 3,772 rows of the sick thyroid data and 75 of the 155 rows of hepatitis. The labels are computed in the full feature space, not in any two-dimensional projection. One verifiable file was not measured: covertype (581,012 rows), which two entries use only as a seven-class file, so that it would give one-vs-rest tasks only, was beyond our computing time. Of the 857 dataset names, 161 have no file in these copies (58 of them name a public source such as UCI or KEEL; the others are private data, sites that no longer exist, image, text and time-series collections, or names that do not identify a data set), 196 are synthetic and 79 have a file whose size differs from every printed one.

Where Reported Wins over SMOTE Come From

At the paper level, 44 of the 73 papers use plain SMOTE as a baseline, 13 use SMOTE inside a multiclass or ensemble scheme, and 16 do not compare with SMOTE at all. Fewer papers give scores a reader can pair: 29 papers print per-dataset scores for the proposed method and plain SMOTE in the same table. For these papers we compared the printed values on every metric that the table reports for both methods, with the classifier and condition fixed as in Section 1.1; a win means the proposed method’s printed value is better in the metric’s direction, and equal printed values count as a tie. This gives 1,511 comparisons on 524 datasets (one to six metrics per paper, median three); 16 cannot be decided because a value is not printed as a number. Of the other 1,495 (520 datasets), the proposed method wins 1,107, ties 102 and loses 286, a win in 79.5% of the decided comparisons (95% CI 77.3 to 81.5). Twenty-three of the 29 papers report at least one comparison that SMOTE wins.

We tested the hypothesis that motivated this analysis: that proposed methods win more often on data the authors modified or generated than on original data. The data do not support it (Table 7). Modified and synthetic data give a win in 75.7% of decided comparisons (373 of 493) against 79.4% on original data. Because the comparisons of one paper are not independent, we estimated the difference with the paper as the unit of clustering: a logistic model with paper-level clustering (generalised estimating equations) gives an odds ratio of 0.69 (95% CI 0.43 to 1.08, \(p = 0.10\)) for modified or synthetic against original data; a conditional logistic model that compares the two kinds of data only inside the 12 papers that use both and report both outcomes gives 0.62 (0.39 to 0.99, \(p = 0.04\)); and a mixed model with random effects for paper and for dataset gives 0.75 (0.58 to 0.98). The direction is therefore the opposite of the hypothesis, but it is not stable: with one result per dataset the two clustered estimates are 0.66 (\(p = 0.19\)) and 0.51 (\(p = 0.17\)), and under the single-metric rule 0.83 (\(p = 0.58\)) and 0.69 (\(p = 0.43\)). Paper by paper, among the 14 papers with both kinds of data, the win share is higher on modified or synthetic data in 4, higher on standard data in 7 and equal in 3 (sign test \(p = 0.55\)). Repository-defined splits do not differ from original data (odds ratio 1.19, \(p = 0.61\)), and the comparisons whose data origin cannot be told show the highest raw win share apart from the two papers with synthetic data, a difference that disappears once papers are taken into account (odds ratio 0.99, \(p = 0.98\)).

The second hypothesis concerned papers that add a single standard dataset to data of another kind. Two papers fit this pattern: MWMOTE (one standard and 19 other datasets) and RUSBoost [seiffert2010rusboost] (one and 14). Both win on their standard dataset; on their modified datasets and those of unstated origin they win 52 of 65 decided comparisons (80.0%; two MWMOTE datasets that could not be matched to a record are left out), the same share as on such data in the 22 papers that have at least two standard datasets and also report other data (484 of 603, 80.3%). Four papers compare with SMOTE only on standard data and one (INOS) only on modified data. Two papers are too few for a test, and nothing in them suggests that the standard dataset serves a different purpose from the rest.

Measured difficulty says more about where the wins fall than the origin of the data. For the 106 verifiable two-class files (Section 1.5) that appear in these comparisons (23 papers, 494 comparisons), the chance that the proposed method beats SMOTE rises with the noise index: the odds ratio per 0.1 of noise index is 1.14 (95% CI 1.03 to 1.27, \(p = 0.009\)) with paper-level clustering and 1.18 (1.04 to 1.33, \(p = 0.009\)) within papers, and 1.20 (1.04 to 1.39, \(p = 0.01\)) with one result per file and paper. The imbalance ratio shows no such relation (odds ratio 0.92 per doubling, \(p = 0.58\)), nor do the small-sample, outlier and small-disjunct flags taken one at a time. This analysis is exploratory: it covers the files that could be verified, which are mostly small and low-dimensional.

Comparisons with SMOTE inside another scheme are kept apart and are not pooled with Tables 6 and 7. Twelve papers contribute 558 comparisons: Static-SMOTE (EMDO [yao2021emdo], OVO-SMOTE, SOUP) 79, with 69 wins, 3 ties and 7 losses; SMOTE after one-versus-one decomposition (AMDO [yang2018amdo], GDHS [yan2025gdhs], SHSampler [zheng2022shsampler]) 148, with 101, 6 and 41; SMOTE applied to all classes (MC-CCR [koziarski2020mcccr], MC-RBO [krawczyk2020mcrbo], NROMM) 239, with 231, 0 and 8; and SMOTE combined with another learner (DSRBF [fernandeznavarro2011dsrbf], EasyEnsemble, GAMO) 92, with 71, 2 and 19. Three papers are left out of every comparison set. KNNOR [islam2022knnor] prints only means over its 19 datasets (G-score .8363 for KNNOR and .8238 for SMOTE). MC-MBRC [ma2024mcmbrc] names SMOTE as a baseline, but the column headers of its per-dataset tables do not say which column is SMOTE. In RBBoost [diezpastor2015randombalance], the scores of its RB-Boost come from the Boosting-family table of its supplement (Supplementary Table 11) and those of its SMOTE ensemble (ESM) from the data-processing-family table (Supplementary Table 3); both report the same protocol (J48 with Laplace smoothing, ensembles of 100, stratified \(5\times2\)-fold cross-validation), but the paper compares methods only within each family and never compares RB-Boost with ESM directly. Its 86 datasets, 63 of them repository-defined, are kept in our data for audit.

What the reader should do.

Read a reported win over SMOTE together with the metric: precision and specificity often favour SMOTE even when the other metrics do not. Expect wins over SMOTE to be more frequent on data whose minority examples are borderline or isolated, and less informative on clean data. Whether the data were modified does not, on this evidence, inflate the win rate; whether they are described well enough to be identified matters more for the reader (Sections 1.4 and 1.7).

Of the 57 papers that use SMOTE as a baseline (44 plain, 13 wrapped), 13 give a reader no per-dataset pair of scores in the paper itself: the results are plots (Borderline-SMOTE [han2005borderline], Safe-Level-SMOTE [bunkhumpornpat2009safelevel], Cluster-SMOTE [cieslak2006cluster], k-means SMOTE [douzas2018kmeans], GLOS [han2023glos]), averages (G-SMOTE [douzas2019gsmote], CISO [yadav2025ciso], SplitBal [sun2015splitbal], QC-SMOTE [upman2026qcsmote]), or ranks (MDO, RBO [koziarski2019rbo], MC-NCLWO [tao2025mcnclwo]), and the review [hassanat2022stop] compares synthetic points rather than classifiers. A fourteenth paper, KNNOR, prints its pair of scores only as a mean over its datasets.

Even where per-dataset tables exist, they do not always cover the datasets a paper lists. In the 43 papers with per-dataset comparisons with SMOTE, 195 of the 1,028 listed dataset entries (19.0%, 95% CI 16.7 to 21.5) have no row in the table that compares the proposed method with SMOTE. Seventy-six of them are sets that seven of these papers generate only for an illustration or a side experiment (described below with the other synthetic data), which are not meant to be compared. Of the other 952 entries, 119 (12.5%, 95% CI 10.5 to 14.8) have no such row, and 12 papers account for all of them, most of all SMOTE-IPF [saez2015smoteipf] (32 of 41) and Loyalty-SMOTE (30 of 59). The gap is largest for synthetic sets (38 of 48) and for entries whose origin cannot be told (44 of 166), and smallest for modified and repository-defined data (5 of 180 and 7 of 189). Some of these datasets appear in other results tables of the same paper; what is missing for them is the pair of scores against SMOTE.

Synthetic data are the hardest to check, because a reader can only regenerate them. In 29 papers, 213 dataset entries are generated data; 93 of them are sets that ten papers generate only for an illustration or a side experiment, which we count as entries as well. Seven papers give a location for those data (63 entries; for example k-means SMOTE [douzas2018kmeans] and G-SMOTE [douzas2019gsmote]), three take them from cited work (13 entries; NROMM reuses the four simulated sets of SVDD-WSMOTE), MC-MBRC [ma2024mcmbrc] states that its 60 generated sets are available on request, RSMOTE names only the generator (3 entries), five link only the code of their method (10 entries), and thirteen say nothing about where the data can be obtained (64 entries, among them the 24 sets of SPIDER2). OREM-M is counted twice: its simulated illustration has no location, while its toy set, which the paper lists without a source, is the synthetic set of the ordinal-regression benchmark [gutierrez2016ordinal]; the public copy has the same 300 examples, two features and five class sizes, so it is an unmodified published set.

Evidence: build/synthetic_scan.py (all 72 PDFs), build/add_synthetic_entries.py (8 Nov 2026: the 93 generated sets of ten papers added as entries, each with a quoted sentence asserted on the cited PDF page) and build/synthetic_availability.py \(\rightarrow\) out/synthetic_availability.json and .csv (29 papers, 213 entries by group; OREM-M in two groups). OREM-M toy: build/full_extraction.py EXTERNAL (public copy github.com/ayrna/orca, exampledata/1-holdout/toy). Supersedes the keyword search of 29 Oct (name_level_extras.py), which had missed the statements of k-means SMOTE and CTGAN.

Baseline results are also reused across papers. QC-SMOTE copies its baseline numbers from the VS-SMOTE paper [qiu2025vssmote], and every SMOTE-all value in MC-CCR’s Table 6 is identical, to two decimals and on all 20 datasets, to the SMOTE-all column of MC-RBO’s Table VI, from the same group and with the same C5.0 setup. The same pattern appears across research groups: the Baseline, SSMOTE, GCS, ABNC, OSMOTE and AMDO columns of EMDO’s Table 5 [yao2021emdo] repeat, value for value on all nine shared datasets, the MAUC results of AMDO’s Table 6 [yang2018amdo]; EMDO states that it uses the same datasets as AMDO but not that the baseline results were copied. Reusing a baseline is efficient, but unless it is stated, a reader cannot tell whether the comparison was run under identical conditions. Several of these papers place per-dataset results on GitHub or in material outside the paper. Where only ranks are given, the paper’s own table can still be informative: in RBO’s Table 2 (CART, no added noise) SMOTE has the better mean G-mean rank, and CISO reports itself statistically equivalent to SMOTE.

For these papers the headline claim cannot be falsified from what is published. This does not mean the claims are wrong; it means a reader cannot tell whether an average improvement comes from consistent gains or from large gains on a few datasets.

Recommendations for Reporting Data

  1. Name the repository and version of every dataset, and whether the full set or a training file was used (Section 1.4).

  2. State which class or classes form the minority and why, in the text and not only in a table (Section 1.3).

  3. Declare every modification (binarisation, class merging, undersampling, noise, dropped attributes) in the data section, and print the size and class counts of the data actually used (Section 1.3).

  4. Give the imbalance-ratio formula, not only its values (Section 1.4).

  5. Report the number of source families alongside the number of datasets, and keep splits of one source together when testing for significance (Section 1.2).

  6. Report per-dataset results for the proposed method and plain SMOTE on every metric used, with standard and modified datasets shown separately (Sections 1.6 and 1.7).

  7. Separate tuning datasets from evaluation datasets, as CISO and LS [cieslak2008ls] do, and run the baselines rather than copying their numbers (Section 1.7).

  8. Report at least one measure of where the minority examples lie (for example the shares of safe, borderline, rare and outlier examples) next to the imbalance ratio (Sections 1.5 and 1.6).

\section{How the SMOTE Literature Uses Data}
\label{sec:data}

A reader who wants to compare two SMOTE variants, or to choose a benchmark for a
new one, needs answers to questions that the papers rarely answer together.
Can the numbers that two papers report on a dataset of the same name be
compared? How broad is the evidence behind the benchmarks the field relies on?
How difficult, beyond the imbalance ratio, are the datasets that can be
checked? When a paper reports that its method beats SMOTE, on what kind of data does
that happen, and can a reader check it? This section answers these questions
from the 1,747 dataset entries and the comparisons with SMOTE that we extracted from the
76 papers of our corpus: 835 under one fixed metric per paper (834 per dataset and one
average over datasets) and 2,497 over every metric the papers report. Three of them (ENN, AdaBoost and one review) contain no
evaluation on data, so counts below use the 73 papers with an
evaluation on data; Tomek links is kept because it illustrates its method on
one synthetic two-class set.

% Claude 29 Oct 2026 (Toon delegated all open decisions): final wording (was \claudedraft)
The central observation is that the evidence for a new oversampler is only as
interpretable as the description of its data, and in this literature that
description is often incomplete: the same name can denote different tasks, many
modifications are not described well enough to be repeated, and 14 of the 57 papers
that use SMOTE as a baseline give no per-dataset pair of scores against it. Where
per-dataset results exist, the proposed method beats plain SMOTE in about four of five
decided comparisons. These wins are not more frequent on data the authors modified,
but they are more frequent on data whose minority examples are borderline or isolated,
and they are much less consistent on precision and specificity than on the other metrics.

\subsection{Extraction Procedure}
\label{sec:data-method}
For every paper we read the full text and any supplementary file in our
collection, and recorded each dataset as printed, including spelling, with
its group in the paper, source repository, size, number of features and
classes, minority and majority counts, and the imbalance ratio where the
paper prints them, together with the table and page they come from. For each
dataset we also recorded how it reached the experiment:
\emph{original} (used as distributed, with its native classes),
\emph{repository-defined} (a two-class split published by a repository such
as KEEL or imbalanced-learn, used as is), \emph{modified} (the authors chose
the minority classes, merged or dropped classes, set a threshold, undersampled
or injected noise), or \emph{synthetic} (generated by the authors). Where a
paper did not state its source, two fixed rules were applied and flagged:
names that follow the KEEL file convention (for example
\texttt{ecoli-0-1\_vs\_5}, \texttt{yeast4}) were labelled repository-defined,
and common names in multiclass papers with no stated change were labelled
original. Two further rules were fixed before counting: a set that is two-class
in its source and is used without comment was labelled original, and a set from
which the authors removed rows (for example, records with missing values) or
attributes was labelled modified. A set whose source the paper does not state, for which it
prints no size, and whose name identifies a public unmodified file was labelled original (four
entries). One label rests on evidence outside the paper: the \texttt{toy} set of
OREM-M, listed without a source, is the synthetic set of the ordinal-regression
benchmark~\pcite{gutierrez2016ordinal} and is labelled synthetic.

For the results we copied, per dataset, the printed score of the proposed
method and of SMOTE from one results table selected by a fixed rule:
G-mean, else AUC, else F-measure, else accuracy; the classifier highlighted
in the abstract, else the first reported; the unperturbed condition. We
recorded values rather than wins so that any definition of a win can be
applied later. From the same table setting we then copied every other metric that the
paper reports for both methods (2,497 dataset-by-metric values in 44 papers); the
fixed-metric values were copied a second time in this pass, independently, and agree
on all 839 rows that both copies contain. Plain SMOTE was distinguished from SMOTE embedded in a
multiclass or ensemble wrapper (Static-SMOTE, OVO-SMOTE~\pcite{fernandez2013analysing}, SMOTE-all,
SMOTE+AdaBoost). Values printed in a paper are never overwritten; corrections
against the source repository are stored beside them with their justification.
Every extracted value was then checked against the PDF a second time: a value
was accepted when the dataset name and its numbers appear on the same line of
the cited page, and every table that is printed as an image or whose text layer
is garbled was read from the rendered page instead. All 1,654 dataset entries
of the first extraction and 835 fixed-metric comparisons passed this check (the 93 sets added on 8 November were checked the same way, with a quoted sentence on the cited page); the values of the other metrics
were read once, from the text layer or the rendered page.
